difficultyReason: One clear move: the physician cites a counterexample to reject a universal claim. Only (C) names that operation; the other choices describe techniques the argument does not use.
stimulus: Physician: Some commentators claim that all widely prescribed medications have been subjected to large-scale, long-term clinical trials before being approved. But this is simply not true. Acetylsalicylic acid, one of the most widely prescribed medications in the world, entered routine clinical use decades before any such trial was conducted on it.

choices.label: A
choices.text: appealing to an authority in order to settle a disputed empirical question

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two cases to show that they should be treated alike

choices.label: C
choices.text: offering a single instance as a counterexample to a universal claim

choices.label: D
choices.text: distinguishing between two senses of a key term used by an opposing side

choices.label: E
choices.text: inferring a general pattern from a representative sample of cases

explanations.correct: The commentators claim every widely prescribed drug went through large-scale trials first. The physician cites one drug that did not, which is exactly how a counterexample refutes a universal claim.
explanations.A: No authority is cited; the physician offers a factual case, not an expert opinion.
explanations.B: Only one case is discussed; no second case is compared to it.
explanations.D: No term is parsed into distinct senses.
explanations.E: The physician is refuting a generalization, not building one from a sample.

difficultyReason: Single move: the ethicist draws an analogy between two cases. Only (B) describes that operation.
stimulus: Ethicist: Many people believe that it is wrong to break a promise to a friend but perfectly acceptable to break a promise to a stranger. But a promise to a stranger, like a promise to a friend, creates an expectation in the person to whom the promise is made. Since breaking a promise to a friend is wrong because it violates such an expectation, breaking a promise to a stranger must be wrong for exactly the same reason.

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing empirical evidence to overturn a widely held moral belief

choices.label: B
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two cases in order to argue that they should be judged alike

choices.label: C
choices.text: appealing to a definition in order to show that a commonly used term is misapplied

choices.label: D
choices.text: pointing out an internal contradiction in an opposing position

choices.label: E
choices.text: generalizing from a single instance to a broad moral principle

explanations.correct: The ethicist identifies a feature shared by both kinds of promises (creating an expectation) and uses the parallel to argue that the moral verdict must be the same. That is the structure of an argument by analogy.
explanations.A: No empirical evidence is introduced; the argument is conceptual.
explanations.C: No definition of any term is offered.
explanations.D: No contradiction within the opposing view is exposed.
explanations.E: The ethicist does not move from one instance to a broad principle; the principle about expectations is a premise, not a conclusion.

difficultyReason: One move: the economist applies a general principle to a specific case to predict an outcome. Only (D) names that operation.
stimulus: Economist: Whenever a government imposes a price ceiling below the market-clearing price for a good, a shortage of that good inevitably develops. The proposed cap on rental prices in our city would set the legal maximum well below the current market rate. So we should expect a shortage of available rental units in our city to follow.

choices.label: A
choices.text: appealing to a historical example in order to predict a future outcome

choices.label: B
choices.text: rejecting a policy proposal by identifying an unintended benefit

choices.label: C
choices.text: inferring a cause from an observed correlation between two variables

choices.label: D
choices.text: applying a general principle to a particular case in order to predict its consequences

choices.label: E
choices.text: distinguishing between short-term and long-term effects of a policy

explanations.correct: The first sentence states a general principle about price ceilings. The economist then shows that the proposed cap fits the description in that principle and concludes about this particular case.
explanations.A: No specific past episode is cited.
explanations.B: The argument predicts a negative effect (shortage), not a benefit.
explanations.C: No correlation is mentioned; the reasoning is principle-to-case, not statistical.

difficultyReason: One move: the attorney appeals to the testimony of a recognized expert to support a factual claim. Only (A) describes that technique.
stimulus: Attorney: The opposing side claims that the fracture in the victim's wrist could have been caused by a simple fall, not by the defendant's grip. But Dr. Ayala, who has served as head of orthopedic trauma at the regional medical center for over twenty years, has testified that fractures of this precise pattern almost never result from falls and are nearly always the product of direct twisting force. So we should accept that the fracture was caused by a twisting grip rather than by a fall.

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing the testimony of a recognized expert to support a factual claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: offering a counterexample to a broad generalization advanced by opponents

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between the present case and a previously decided one

choices.label: D
choices.text: rejecting an opposing claim by showing that it rests on a contradiction

choices.label: E
choices.text: arguing from the absence of evidence to the truth of a positive claim

explanations.correct: The attorney's sole support for the conclusion is Dr. Ayala's credentials and testimony. That is a textbook appeal to expert authority.
explanations.B: No single case is cited against a universal claim; the argument relies on expert statements, not instances.
explanations.C: No previously decided case is introduced.
explanations.D: The opposing side's position is not shown to contradict itself.
explanations.E: The attorney relies on positive expert testimony, not on a gap in evidence.

difficultyReason: One move: the ecologist offers an alternative explanation for an observed decline. Only (E) describes that operation.
stimulus: Ecologist: Some researchers have argued that the recent decline in the population of native songbirds in our region must be due to increased pesticide use on nearby farms. But there is another possibility that deserves serious consideration: over the same period, the population of feral house cats in the region has more than doubled, and feral cats are well-documented predators of songbirds.
questionStem: The ecologist responds to the researchers' argument by

choices.label: A
choices.text: offering an alternative explanation for the phenomenon the researchers have identified

choices.label: B
choices.text: denying that the phenomenon the researchers describe has actually occurred

choices.label: C
choices.text: pointing out that the researchers' evidence is drawn from an unrepresentative sample

choices.label: D
choices.text: showing that the researchers' conclusion contradicts another of their own claims

choices.label: E
choices.text: citing a counterexample that undermines the researchers' general principle

explanations.correct: The ecologist accepts that the songbird population has declined and that it needs explaining, but proposes cat predation as a rival cause to pesticide use. That is an alternative-explanation move.
explanations.B: The ecologist does not dispute the decline.
explanations.D: No contradiction within the researchers' position is identified.
explanations.E: The ecologist does not refute a universal claim with a single instance; the move is to supply a competing cause.

difficultyReason: One move: the engineer distinguishes between two cases the critic has treated as equivalent. Only (C) names that technique.
stimulus: Software engineer: Critics of our new messaging platform argue that because our earlier video-conferencing product suffered from frequent connection failures, the new platform will suffer from similar problems. But the earlier product relied on a centralized server architecture, whereas the new messaging platform uses a peer-to-peer architecture in which no single server's failure can disrupt communication. The critics' inference therefore does not go through.
questionStem: The software engineer's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: rejecting a claim by showing that accepting it leads to absurd consequences

choices.label: B
choices.text: conceding a critic's premise while denying that the conclusion follows from it alone

choices.label: C
choices.text: distinguishing between two cases in order to show that a comparison between them is unwarranted

choices.label: D
choices.text: citing statistical evidence to undermine an anecdotal generalization

choices.label: E
choices.text: offering a definition that shows a key term has been misapplied

explanations.correct: The critics lump the two products together. The engineer's entire move is to identify a relevant difference in architecture that breaks the analogy the critics rely on.
explanations.B: The engineer does not concede the critics' analogy; he rejects it outright by showing the cases differ.

difficultyReason: One clean move: the linguist appeals to a definition to argue that a term has been misapplied. Only (B) describes that technique.
stimulus: Linguist: Commentators in the popular press routinely describe the way young people use the word "literally" as a grammatical error. But a grammatical error is, by definition, a violation of the structural rules governing word order and inflection in a language. The pattern in question involves neither word order nor inflection; it is simply a shift in the meaning speakers attach to a particular word. So whatever else one may say about it, it is not a grammatical error.

choices.label: A
choices.text: citing empirical data about usage to refute a prescriptive claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: appealing to a definition in order to show that a term has been misapplied

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy to a parallel case in another language

choices.label: D
choices.text: identifying an unstated assumption in an opposing argument and rejecting it

choices.label: E
choices.text: generalizing from several instances to a rule about a broad class of cases

explanations.correct: The linguist offers a definition of "grammatical error" and then argues that the phenomenon the commentators describe does not fall under it. That is an appeal to definition to show misapplication of a term.
explanations.A: No usage data or statistics are invoked.
explanations.C: No second language or parallel case appears.
explanations.D: The linguist doesn't surface a hidden assumption; she relies on the meaning of a term.
explanations.E: The argument moves from a definition to a case, not from instances to a rule.

difficultyReason: One move: the historian supports a general claim by generalizing from representative cases. Only (D) describes that operation.
stimulus: Historian: Nearly every major technological transition in the past three centuries — the shift from water power to steam, from steam to electricity, and from electricity to electronics — was accompanied by a substantial, if temporary, rise in unemployment in the industries being displaced. Given this consistent pattern, it is reasonable to expect that major technological transitions in general will be accompanied by similar temporary unemployment.

choices.label: A
choices.text: distinguishing between short-term effects and long-term effects of a single trend

choices.label: B
choices.text: applying a general principle to a particular case in order to predict an outcome

choices.label: C
choices.text: rejecting an opposing explanation by offering a competing one

choices.label: D
choices.text: generalizing from a series of cases that exhibit a common pattern

choices.label: E
choices.text: citing an authoritative source to support a contested empirical claim

explanations.correct: The historian lists several past technological transitions, notes that each shared a feature, and on that basis extends the pattern to technological transitions as a class.
explanations.A: No long-term effect is contrasted with a short-term one; the argument is about the general pattern.
explanations.B: The move runs the other direction: from cases to a general expectation, not from a principle to a case.

difficultyReason: One clear move: the policy analyst rejects a proposal by showing that the principle behind it leads to an absurd consequence. Only (E) describes that technique.
stimulus: Policy analyst: The council has proposed requiring background checks before anyone may buy any item that could conceivably be used to harm another person. But the principle behind this proposal — that we should screen purchasers of anything that could conceivably be used to cause harm — would equally require us to screen buyers of kitchen knives, garden shears, heavy hammers, and even rolls of duct tape. Clearly, then, the proposal cannot be accepted as it stands.
questionStem: The policy analyst's argument proceeds by

choices.label: A
choices.text: offering a counterexample that falsifies a universal empirical claim

choices.label: B
choices.text: appealing to expert testimony to cast doubt on a legislative proposal

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between the proposal and a successful policy in another jurisdiction

choices.label: D
choices.text: distinguishing between two categories of items that the proposal fails to separate

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejecting a proposal by showing that the principle behind it has unacceptable consequences

explanations.correct: The analyst extracts the principle implicit in the proposal, shows that applying it consistently would require screening kitchen knives and duct tape, and treats that outcome as reason to reject the proposal. That is the structure of a reductio-style objection.
explanations.A: The claim being attacked is a policy recommendation, not a universal empirical claim.
explanations.C: No other jurisdiction's policy is introduced.
explanations.D: The analyst lumps items together to embarrass the proposal rather than distinguishing categories within it.

difficultyReason: One move: the curator draws a conclusion about an individual work from a general claim about a class it belongs to. Only (A) describes that technique.
stimulus: Curator: Every painting produced by the Delft workshop during the 1660s was executed on a panel of oak imported from the Baltic region. The small landscape that has just been donated to our museum was, as our own laboratory has confirmed, produced by the Delft workshop during the 1660s. So the panel on which it was painted must be Baltic oak.

choices.label: A
choices.text: applying a generalization about a class of objects to a particular member of that class

choices.label: B
choices.text: inferring a general claim about a class of objects from information about one of its members

choices.label: C
choices.text: drawing an analogy between two objects in order to argue that they share a feature

choices.label: D
choices.text: citing expert testimony to resolve a disagreement about a historical fact

choices.label: E
choices.text: rejecting a hypothesis about an object by appealing to a counterexample

explanations.correct: The curator starts from a general statement about every painting produced by the Delft workshop in the 1660s, identifies the donated painting as a member of that class, and concludes that it must have the property the generalization ascribes to the class.
explanations.B: The argument runs in the opposite direction — from a generalization to a particular case.
explanations.C: No second object is introduced for comparison.
explanations.D: The laboratory's confirmation establishes membership in the class but is not used to resolve a dispute about a historical fact.
explanations.E: No hypothesis is being refuted; the curator is establishing, not refuting, a claim.
